messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Vignette:
Julian Vance grew up in a house where affection was mediated through the unpredictable physical aggression of the man who raised him. He cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to himself; the memories refuse to align into a coherent timeline. When fragments of those years surface, he sometimes can recall what happened but feels completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger. Yet, when he remembers the event he feels intense guilt, a heavy, inescapable weight that settles in his chest. That guilt circles alongside his dwelling on what other people have done to him, and alongside his dwelling on what he has done wrong. Neither rumination yields; they simply occupy his quiet hours, turning over in his mind until he stops trying to sleep. He has built his evenings around avoiding situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, keeping his apartment brightly lit, pacing the kitchen, and refusing to lie down before midnight. Now fifty-five, Julian runs a small fashion design studio in a converted warehouse downtown. The space should be his sanctuary, yet even inside his own home, he feels on guard. His days are filled with the careful architecture of fabrics and fittings, but the studio is where his body keeps rehearsing old warnings. When an assistant reaches past him to steady a bolt of silk, or when a pattern maker pats his shoulder to draw attention to a seam, he reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly. His shoulders hike, his breath catches, and it takes deliberate effort to smooth his expression. The studio’s usual hum of machines and chatter is manageable, but when the room goes quiet, the unusual silence makes him feel something dangerous is about to happen. He cannot explain why, but the absence of noise feels like a held breath before impact, so he immediately fills the gaps with instructions, with music, with movement. He has come to believe he has permanently changed for the worse, that the man he was has been eroded into someone who flinches at sudden movement. He is certain that people can't be trusted, especially those who offer help without warning. What terrified him most was the conviction that his reactions since the event mean that he is going crazy, that his tightening chest and jumping pulse prove his mind is fracturing. Over the years, these reactions have shaped his routines and his relationships without speaking to one another. His divorce left little room for negotiation, and now he navigates his days with careful distance. The consequences are practical and concrete: he leaves the studio early, skips evening gatherings, and cancels meetings when his hands tremble during fittings. Clients notice his unavailability, and former colleagues remark on how he withdraws when conversations grow quiet. Julian does not see these patterns as linked mechanisms; he sees them as necessary, parallel defenses. He simply exists in a state of bracing, where the past bleeds into the present and his nervous system keeps pace with a threat that no longer has a face. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single breaking point, but a slow accumulation of exhaustion. He found himself staring at a patterned textile for hours, paralyzed by the ghost of a voice that no longer exists, unable to reconstruct how he had arrived there. He came to the clinic hoping to understand why his body keeps bracing for violence in a room that offers none, and what he might do if he ever allowed himself to remember without drowning in guilt. He is most afraid that his reactions will only grow stranger, that the lines between past and present will blur until he can no longer work or trust his own judgment. Yet, beneath the fear, he hopes to find a way to sit in a quiet room without feeling threatened, to let his hands move through fabric without bracing, and to finally tell his own story without flinching.
